name: Eboymaxxing

lead: Eboymaxxing is the practice of dressing and styling oneself in the e-boy aesthetic, a TikTok-era youth style built around longer center-parted curtain hair, layered tops, dark or monochrome outfits and accessories such as chains. In looksmaxxing circles it is treated as a style meta: a way to frame the face with hair and to present a recognisable, youthful look.

The e-boy subculture itself is documented by encyclopedias and fashion press as emerging in the late 2010s from emo, scene and mall-goth fashion mixed with Japanese and Korean street styles. No studies have tested whether the look changes rated attractiveness; the wiki-community claim is that it suits younger men with thick hair.

paras: Practitioners grow the hair out to roughly ear or chin length, part it down the middle and style it with products such as sea-salt spray or mousse, often using a blow-dryer and comb to make the split sit naturally. Some use a perm for curly variants. Clothing is layered (band tees over striped long sleeves, oversized sweaters), with chains and similar accessories. A looksmax.org guide says the hair took around four months to grow out.

The look carries few physical risks. Growing hair out takes months, heat-styling can dry hair, and the aesthetic is tied to youth trends that shift quickly. Forum replies describe it as best suited to teenagers and people under about 20.

angle.text: Practitioners use the curtain cut to frame the face, and layered clothing and accessories to present a cohesive style. The changes are reversible and based on hair length and clothing.

lead: Eboymaxxing is the looksmaxxing term for adopting the e-boy aesthetic, a youth style popularised on TikTok that combines center-parted curtain hair, layered or oversized clothing and accessories. It is used as a way to improve appearance through hair and styling rather than through surgery or medication.[1][2]

The underlying subculture grew out of emo, scene and mall-goth fashion mixed with Japanese and South Korean street style, and received mainstream attention after TikTok's worldwide release in 2018 and during 2019 to 2020.[2] Mainstream outlets have since published guides to the 'eboy curtain haircut', and fashion houses released collections described as e-boy inspired.[2][3]

A looksmax.org guide advises that the look is intended for teenagers rated about 5 PSL or higher, and lays out haircut options (curtains, curly perm) and styling steps.[1] No clinical or perception studies of the e-boy look exist.
infobox: Emo, scene, mall goth, Asian street fashion[2]

paras: The e-boy aesthetic is characterised by curtained hair, oversized sweaters, monochrome outfits, band merchandise layered over striped long-sleeve shirts and polo necks, with chain necklaces, wallet chains and earrings as accessories.[2] Heavy makeup such as blush and eyeliner appears in parts of the scene.[2]

The curtain haircut is described by L'Oreal Paris's beauty magazine as a longer style that usually reaches about ear level, with a center part and curtain bangs, and as working on textures from straight to curly.[3]

The e-girl and e-boy subculture emerged in the late 2010s, drawing on emo, scene and mall goth and on Japanese and South Korean street fashion. Business Insider traced early e-girls to Tumblr.[2] Interest rose after TikTok's worldwide release in 2018, and 'transformation' videos where users turned into e-boys or e-girls spread in 2019.[2]

In 2020 'e-girl style' ranked among Google's top trending fashion terms, and designers including Celine and Ludovic de Saint Sernin showed e-boy-influenced collections in late 2020 and early 2021.[2] Lil Peep and Yungblud are named among musicians associated with the style.[2]

A looksmax.org guide titled as an ultimate eboymaxxing guide recommends beginning with the haircut, trying several variants to see which suits the face. It describes the curtain style as taking around four months to grow, using a hairdryer and comb to split the hair, and sea-salt spray for volume on thin hair; a curly perm variant is described for people with thick hair.[1]
Haircare guides add styling options including gel for a wet look, mousse and a diffuser for curls, a round brush to flip the ends outward, and pomade or putty for a messy finish.[3]

The guide's author limits the recommendation to teenagers in high school with already high facial ratings.[1] Replies in the thread joke about the label and say it is most useful for people under about 20.[1] Wikipedia notes criticism of the wider subculture, including its pejorative origins and sexualised content, and musician James Blake's criticism of the 'sad boy' label.[2]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the e-boy look is discussed as a style meta suited to younger users with a good hairline and thick hair.[1]

claims.claim: The e-boy haircut is the optimal style for teenagers.

timeline.event: TikTok's worldwide release; e-girl and e-boy subculture gains mainstream attention.[2]
E-girl style among Google's top trending fashion terms; Celine collection influenced by e-boys.[2]
